title: A 30-Year-Old Flew Home from Boston to Lead India's Biggest Youth Protest in a Decade
excerpt: The Cockroach Janta Party, born from a social media insult 21 days ago, held its first on-ground rally at Jantar Mantar. It has 22 million Instagram followers and one demand: the Education Minister must go.
body:
Abhijeet Dipke landed at Delhi airport on Saturday morning, walked straight to Jantar Mantar, and stood on a stage before thousands of people who had come to demand the resignation of India's Education Minister. He is 30 years old. He has lived in Boston for the past two years, a common path for many young Indians seeking professional opportunities abroad, yet his return underscores the deep ties and civic engagement many in the diaspora maintain with developments back home, especially those affecting India's youth and future. The movement he founded — the Cockroach Janta Party — is 21 days old and has 22 million Instagram followers.

It was the largest on-ground youth protest in India in years, and it was born from an insult.

From Slur to Movement

The name started as a jab. About a month ago, critics of students who were questioning India's examination system called them cockroaches and parasites — unworthy of being heard, meant to be crushed underfoot. Dipke, who had been following the NEET paper leak scandal and the CBSE On-Screen Marking controversy from the United States, posted a response on social media.

"What would happen if all the cockroaches came together?" he asked.

The response from Generation Z was overwhelming. Within days, the social media account "Cockroach is Back" had millions of followers. A loosely structured organization took shape, with Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka emerging as spokespeople. They had one demand: Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan must resign.

Saturday's protest at Jantar Mantar — New Delhi's designated protest site — was the movement's first test in the physical world. Police deployed over 1,000 personnel across the capital. Barricades went up on surrounding roads. Protesters wore cockroach masks and T-shirts. Banners read "We asked for Make in India, you gave us Leak in India" and "Dharmendra Pradhan isteefa do."

The Government's Response

The Modi government has not ignored the movement. It has blocked CJP's X account within India, a decision the group has challenged in a Delhi high court. Senior cabinet minister Kiren Rijiju has accused the organization of seeking followers from Pakistan and what he called the "anti-India gang."

Dipke told reporters that his family and friends had feared he could be arrested on his return to India. Delhi Police granted permission for the demonstration only after meeting Dipke at the airport.

"This is a peaceful movement for the youth of the nation," said Ranka at Jantar Mantar on Saturday.

Not a Party. A Moment.

Political strategist Yogendra Yadav, writing on X, cautioned against judging the Cockroach Janta Party by conventional political standards.

"Cockroach Janta Party is not really a political party. It is simply ordinary people coming together. It is not a movement; it is a moment, and that is why it matters," he wrote.

Senior journalist Smita Gupta sees it differently. She believes the movement has emerged at precisely the moment when public enthusiasm for the Modi government has begun to fade. Unlike earlier student movements at JNU that focused on abstract ideals like democracy and free expression, CJP's concerns — examination integrity, recruitment fraud, youth unemployment — are visceral. They affect students and their parents equally, and resonate deeply within the Indian diaspora, many of whom have family members directly impacted or who consider India for their children's education and careers.

"The concerns raised by CJP are directly linked to the everyday lives of young people and their families," she said. The comparison to Anna Hazare's anti-corruption movement of 2011, which eventually birthed the Aam Aadmi Party, is already being made openly.

Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk joined the protest after stating publicly that he would attend if the Education Minister did not resign by June 5.

'Unkillable, Like a Cockroach'

The movement's trajectory will depend on what happens next. CJP has given the government a one-week ultimatum. If Pradhan does not step down, Ranka said, the movement will return to Jantar Mantar the following Saturday.

Some analysts are skeptical. Political commentator Sharad Gupta argues that the movement lacks experienced leadership and a clear strategy beyond its single demand. "This anger is focused on Dharmendra Pradhan today. Tomorrow it may be directed at someone else," he said.

But CJP's founders have leaned into the name they were given. A cockroach, they note, is one of the most resilient creatures on earth. It survives everything.

"It is a gathering of young people. It is a youth movement," Ranka said at Jantar Mantar. When asked whether the group would enter electoral politics, he answered with a question of his own: "The air we breathe, the water we drink, and the schools where we study are all political. So what is political and what is not?"
image_caption: Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, whose resignation is the central demand of the Cockroach Janta Party
author: Diaspora Desk
